title: La Bohème
facts: La Bohème premiered on 1 February 1896 at the Teatro Regio in Turin, conducted by the 28-year-old Arturo Toscanini.
The first-night audience was subdued, and the critics were divided.
Toscanini conducted it again on radio in 1946, 50 years after the premiere. It is the only recording of a Puccini opera by its original conductor.
Ruggero Leoncavallo claimed he had offered Puccini a finished Bohème libretto. Puccini said he hadn't known and wouldn't abandon his own opera, so Leoncavallo wrote a rival Bohème.
Leoncavallo’s rival version swapped the voices: his Marcello is a tenor and his Rodolfo a baritone.
“Che gelida manina” was recorded by nearly 500 tenors in at least seven languages between 1900 and 1980.
Enrico Caruso, closely associated with Rodolfo, recorded this aria in 1906.
Rodolfo turns to see Mimì bathed in moonlight, and their voices join in “O soave fanciulla”.
Act II opens at the Café Momus with a big crowd, children included, and street sellers calling out their wares.
In this quartet, Mimì and Rodolfo part tenderly while Marcello and Musetta quarrel fiercely about her flirting.
O Mimì, tu più|O Mimi, tu piu
“O Mimì, tu più non torni”: Rodolfo and Marcello, both alone again, are nostalgic for their lost loves.
When news of Puccini’s death reached Rome in 1924, a Bohème performance was stopped and the orchestra played Chopin’s Funeral March.
The Met first staged La Bohème on 26 December 1900, with Nellie Melba as Mimì.
La Bohème was the last opera performed in the Met’s original 1883 building, on 16 April 1966.
Benjamin Britten wrote in 1951 that after four or five performances he never wanted to hear Bohème again.
The musical Rent, winner of the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, is based on La Bohème.
Moonstruck (1987) used the 1959 Bohème recording with Renata Tebaldi and Carlo Bergonzi on its soundtrack.
